title: LED blink — deterministic test fixture
summary: Deterministic test fixture, not an AI-generated answer. Arduino Uno D9 supplies 5 V logic through a 220-ohm resistor and a red LED with 2 V forward drop; LED cathode connects to GND.
objectives: Explain LED polarity and series current limiting.
Program one second on and one second off.

components.name: Breadboard
components.details: Use separate connected strips; check the board layout.

components.name: Red LED
components.details: Forward voltage 2 V; maximum current 20 mA.

components.name: 220-ohm resistor
components.details: Keep it in series with the LED.

components.name: Jumper wires
components.details: Use wires for the stated series connections.

expectedResults: Approximate LED current is (5 V - 2 V) / 220 ohms = 0.013636 A, or 13.6 mA.
LED alternates one second on and one second off.
uncertainties: This fixture does not electrically verify a circuit or test the suggested code.

steps.title: Check the declared ratings
steps.instruction: Use the declared 5 V output, 2 V LED drop and 220-ohm resistor. Calculate (5 - 2) / 220 = 0.013636 A, approximately 13.6 mA.
steps.why: The series resistor limits current below the declared 20 mA maximum.
steps.check: Why must the resistor stay in series?

steps.title: Wire with simulation stopped
steps.instruction: Connect D9 to one end of the 220-ohm resistor, its other end to the LED anode, and the LED cathode to GND. Check polarity and connected breadboard strips.
steps.why: Correct polarity and current limiting are necessary for this series path.
steps.check: Can you trace D9 through the resistor and LED to GND?

steps.title: Add the suggested blink program
steps.instruction: Use the untested suggested code below. D9 turns on for 1000 milliseconds, then off for 1000 milliseconds.
steps.why: Pin mode enables output and the two delays set the blink interval.
steps.check: What does 1000 milliseconds mean in seconds?

steps.title: Observe the simulated result
steps.instruction: After checking the connections and resistor, start the simulation yourself and observe the intended one-second blink intervals.
steps.why: Observation can reveal mistakes; this guide cannot claim your actual circuit is electrically verified.
steps.check: If the LED does not blink, stop simulation and inspect wiring, polarity and code.
